title: File:Yum pladook foo.jpg
author: Takeaway
description:
Yam pladuk fu (Thai: ยำปลาดุกฟู): salad of "fluffy" catfish.
The dish is made with dried catfish (pladuk, Thai: ปลาดุก) which has first been shredded and then deep fried until crispy. It can be topped with a salad made from thinly sliced green (unripe and tangy) mango, shallots, fish sauce, chillies, lime juice, sugar and coriander leaves, or as seen here, the salad served on the side to prevent the crispy fish from turning soggy.

It can be eaten as a snack, a starter, or as one of the main course dishes of a full meal.

author: PattayaPatrol
description: This is a beautifully plated Thai-style glass noodle salad, often known as "Yum Woon Sen." The dish features transparent glass noodles topped with plump pink shrimp, fresh sliced tomatoes, and bright green cilantro leaves. On the side of the plate, there are decoratively carved cucumber slices with their characteristic ridged edges. The salad likely has a tangy, spicy dressing typical of Thai cuisine, made with ingredients such as lime juice, fish sauce, and chili. The combination of colors - the pink shrimp, red tomatoes, green herbs, and translucent noodles - creates a visually appealing presentation on the dark plate.

author: El Mono Español
description:
ESPAÑA, GRECIA, ITALIA, PORTUGAL Y TURQUÍA
Se lavan los calamares en agua fría y se dejan
escurrir en un colador. Lo más común es cortar el
calamar en anillos, pero también puede hacerse en
tiras. Las patas también se aprovechan, y se pue-
den freír así enteras o si son muy grandes se cortan
por la mitad. En un plato grande se pone harina y
se enharinan los trozos de calamar por todos sus
lados. En una sartén profunda, se calienta aceite
de oliva y se fríe todo hasta que alcance un color
dorado. Cuando esté listo, se pasa unos minutos a
un plato con papel de cocina para retirar el exceso
de aceite. Finalmente, se salan y se sirve aún

caliente con gajos de limón.

title: File:Moo nam tok.jpg
groups: ลาบและน้ำตก
author: Takeaway
description:
Mu nam tok (Thai: หมูน้ำตก): nam tok means waterfall in Thai, mu is pork. The dish is originally from northeastern Thailand (Isan).
There are several explanations why this dish is called this way and none are satisfactory. A plausible theory is that the meat should still contain blood, which will run out from it, when sliced, as a waterfall.
The version shown is the quick version where sliced pork is cooked shortly and then mixed in with the spicy sauce and herbs. The more elaborate version calls for the pork to be grilled first until pink and then sliced and mixed in with the sauce and herbs. The last version is correctly called mu yang nam tok (Thai: ย่าง, yang = grilled). You can also find nuea nam tok and nuea yang nam tok using beef instead of pork.

The sauce is made with ground roasted rice, ground dried chillies, fish sauce, lime juice, shallots and mint leaves. This one also features some spring onions. It is traditionally eaten with sticky rice.
